lead: A battery charger is a controlled DC source that pushes current into a battery along a set profile. It does not simply connect a transformer and a diode; it regulates current, then voltage, and stops at the right point. The same switching devices and sensing circuits run emergency lamps, light dimmers and simple timers. You meet them in phone chargers, inverter packs, stairwell lights and theatre exit signs. This chapter shows the profiles, the regulator loops and the changeover that keeps a lamp alive when the mains fails.
prereq: You need: diode rectifiers with capacitor filters, the buck and flyback converters (DC-DC converters), and phase control of AC voltage controllers. The charger-battery-inverter chain also appears in Uninterruptible power supplies (UPS).

blocks.text: The charging profile depends on cell chemistry, temperature and duty.
C-rate scales current to capacity. For a battery of capacity C Ah, nC means n × C amperes. A 100 Ah battery at 0.1C takes 10 A, not 100 A. Ideally 0.1C fills or empties it in about 10 h.

Charge efficiency η is Ah output divided by Ah input. Lead-acid is about 0.90. You push in more Ah than you took out. The charge factor is F = Ah<sub>in</sub> / Ah<sub>out</sub> = 1/η. To replace 50 Ah at η = 0.90, push in 50/0.90 = 55.6 Ah.

items: Trickle: a small current, often C/100, holds a full battery against self-discharge.
Constant current (CC): fixed current while voltage rises.
Constant voltage (CV): fixed voltage while current falls.
CC-CV: CC to a voltage limit, then CV until current tapers to a termination value. Both stages put charge in: the CC stage returns most of it, the CV stage the rest.
Float versus boost: float is lower standby voltage; boost is higher cycle voltage. A 12 V lead-acid block often floats at 13.5–13.8 V and boosts at 14.4 V.
Pulse charging: current pulses with rest gaps; it reduces polarization but needs control.

blocks.text: Temperature changes the safe voltage. The charger senses battery temperature and reduces or stops charge when hot. Overcharge causes gassing, heat and short life. Termination can be a timer, a current threshold, a voltage drop (dV/dt) or a temperature limit.

Three power stages are common. A series pass regulator puts a transistor between rectified DC and the battery. It drops excess voltage, so it is simple and quiet but wastes (V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>batt</sub>) × I as heat. A buck converter chops and filters; it is efficient for step-down. A flyback gives isolation from mains.

Sensing closes the loops. A current-sense resistor R<sub>s</sub> converts current to voltage: V<sub>s</sub> = I × R<sub>s</sub>. R<sub>s</sub> is small, often milliohms, so it wastes little power. An amplifier raises V<sub>s</sub>. A divider senses battery voltage: V<sub>sense</sub> = V<sub>batt</sub> × R2/(R1 + R2).
P<sub>loss</sub> is heat in W; V<sub>in</sub> is input DC in V; V<sub>batt</sub> is battery voltage in V; I is charge current in A.

items: Rectify and filter the mains (a diode bridge and a capacitor).
Compare both with references; the lower demand wins, so CC runs until the voltage limit, then CV.
Drive the pass device with a linear signal or PWM duty cycle.
Stop at termination; protect against reverse polarity, overcurrent and over-temperature.

blocks.text: A charge controller IC does these steps. A small emergency light may use a linear regulator with a timer. In a UPS, the charger holds a large battery on a DC bus.

An emergency lighting fitting has a lamp, a battery, a charger and a changeover circuit. A maintained fitting keeps its lamp on during normal mains and on battery. A non-maintained fitting keeps the lamp off until mains fails. Exit signs in a cinema are often maintained; a stairwell lamp may be non-maintained.

An inverter tube pack drives a fluorescent tube from a low-voltage battery. The charger is a rectifier plus regulator. With mains present, a relay or static switch keeps the inverter off and charges the battery. On failure, changeover starts the inverter. LED (light-emitting diode) emergency drivers use a constant-current supply; a battery and boost converter take over on mains failure. Each fitting is rated for a duration that the local building code sets; 1 h and 3 h ratings are common.

Changeover can be a relay or a static switch. Transfer must be fast enough that the lamp does not extinguish. A test button breaks the mains input to simulate failure. A self-test checks battery voltage under load, not just open-circuit voltage. A weak battery can read 12 V with no load and collapse under a lamp. Over-discharge protection cuts the lamp before damage.

A phase-control dimmer switches the AC wave partway through each half-cycle. A TRIAC is a bidirectional thyristor switch. A DIAC is a bidirectional trigger diode. A DIAC and an RC network generate the gate pulse. The firing angle α is measured from the zero crossing. A later α gives a shorter conduction angle and a lower root-mean-square (RMS) voltage. This is the ordinary fan regulator and incandescent dimmer. Phase control creates harmonics and radio noise, so a filter is needed. AC voltage controllers treat the waveforms in full.

An electronic timer uses a 555 IC or a comparator. In monostable mode the output pulse is t = 1.1 R C. R is in ohms, C in farads, t in seconds. A zero-crossing detector synchronizes the timer to the mains. The timer drives a relay, a TRIAC or a solid-state relay. Zero-crossing switching reduces electromagnetic interference (EMI) because current starts at zero.

examples.question: A 12 V, 100 Ah lead-acid battery is at 50 % depth of discharge. It is charged at 0.1C in constant current until it reaches 14.4 V, which happens when 80 % of the needed charge is back in. It is then held at 14.4 V while the current falls roughly linearly from the CC value to 2 A, where the charger stops. Charge efficiency is 90 %. Find the constant-current time, the constant-voltage time, the total time and the charger output power at the start and end of the constant-voltage stage.
steps: Charge to push in: Ah<sub>in</sub> = 50 / 0.90 = 55.56 Ah (charge factor 1/0.90 = 1.11).
CC stage returns 80 %: 0.80 × 55.56 = 44.44 Ah, so t<sub>CC</sub> = 44.44 / 10 = 4.44 h.
CV stage returns the rest: 55.56 − 44.44 = 11.11 Ah. With the current falling linearly from 10 A to 2 A, the average is (10 + 2) / 2 = 6 A, so t<sub>CV</sub> = 11.11 / 6 = 1.85 h.
Total time = 4.44 + 1.85 = 6.30 h, about 6 h 18 min.
Charger output power: at the start of CV, P = 14.4 × 10 = 144 W; at the end, P = 14.4 × 2 = 28.8 W.
examples.answer: CC for 4.44 h, CV for 1.85 h, 6.30 h in all; the charger gives 144 W at the start of the CV stage and 28.8 W at its end.

examples.question: A fan-regulator style TRIAC dimmer feeds a 100 W, 230 V incandescent lamp from 230 V, 50 Hz mains. Treat the lamp as a fixed resistance. Find the lamp voltage and power at firing angles of 90° and 120°.
steps: Lamp resistance: R = V² / P = 230² / 100 = 529 Ω.
For a TRIAC fired at α in both half cycles, V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> √(1 − α/π + sin 2α / (2π)), with α in radians and V<sub>s</sub> the supply RMS voltage.
P = 101.7² / 529 = 19.6 W. Check: P is also 100 W × 0.1955 = 19.6 W, because power goes as the square of the RMS voltage.
examples.answer: At α = 90° the lamp gets 162.6 V and 50 W; at α = 120° it gets 101.7 V and 19.6 W.
examples.check:
import math
for a in (90,120):
 r=math.radians(a); k=1-r/math.pi+math.sin(2*r)/(2*math.pi)
 print(a, round(k,4), round(230*math.sqrt(k),1), round(100*k,1))

traps: Reading 0.1C as 100 A for a 100 Ah battery. 0.1C is 10 A.
Forgetting charge efficiency. A 50 Ah discharge needs about 55.6 Ah of charge at 90% efficiency.
Adding a fixed taper time on top of a CC time that already returns all the charge. The CV stage also puts charge in, so the CC stage ends before the full Ah are back.
In a dimmer, thinking a later firing angle raises the RMS voltage. It lowers it.

quiz.a: C-rate is current scaled to capacity: nC = n × C amperes for a C Ah battery. A 100 Ah battery at 0.1C takes 10 A.

quiz.q: Why does a CC-CV charger switch from CC to CV?
quiz.a: CC pushes the required charge quickly. At the voltage limit, CV holds the safe voltage and lets current taper, so overcharge is avoided.

quiz.q: A 12 V, 80 Ah battery is at 40 % depth of discharge. It is charged at 0.1C with η = 0.90. The CC stage returns 80 % of the needed charge, then the current falls linearly to 1.6 A. Find the CC time, the CV time and the total time.
Why is the current-sense resistor in a charger made small?
quiz.a: It converts current to voltage for control. A small R<sub>s</sub> wastes less I²R<sub>s</sub> power and heat, but the amplifier must handle a small signal.

quiz.q: State the difference between maintained and non-maintained emergency lighting.
quiz.a: Maintained: lamp is on during normal mains and on battery. Non-maintained: lamp is off until mains fails.

quiz.q: A 555 monostable has R = 100 kΩ and C = 10 µF. Find the output pulse width.

beyond: Not for the exam. Digital charge controllers use a microcontroller with coulomb counting and battery models, and GaN devices allow small, cool chargers. Search for battery management IC, CC-CV controller and DALI emergency lighting.
